dialect.guess: GnuCOBOL (OpenCOBOL) or similar open-source COBOL, likely targeting a Linux/Unix environment given the JMA ORCA project context
evidence: IDENTIFICATION DIVISION / ENVIRONMENT DIVISION / DATA DIVISION / PROCEDURE DIVISION all present
ORGANIZATION IS INDEXED / ACCESS MODE IS DYNAMIC / RECORD KEY / FILE STATUS clauses
COPY with REPLACING using // delimiters (common in GnuCOBOL/OpenCOBOL)
No EXEC SQL or EXEC CICS
PROGRAM-ID ORCR1010 matches JMA ORCA open-source medical receipt software project

purpose.summary: This program is part of the JMA (Japan Medical Association) ORCA open-source medical receipt software system. It processes public medical insurance receipt data (specifically for outpatient/inpatient claims), performing point/score aggregation by diagnosis category. It reads and writes indexed ISAM files (RECE100, RECE120, RECE130) and produces error output.
purpose.domain: healthcare/medical billing (Japanese national health insurance claims processing)

notable_features: COPY statements with REPLACING using // delimiter syntax (GnuCOBOL style)
Multiple indexed ISAM files with DYNAMIC access mode
Extensive Japanese-language comments encoded in latin-1 (actually EUC-JP or Shift-JIS, decoded as latin-1 producing mojibake)
Large working-storage section with many flag and counter areas (PIC 9(01) flags)
No COMP-3 packed decimal usage despite financial calculations
No EXEC SQL or EXEC CICS
7 CALL statements, 199 PERFORM statements indicating modular structure
Error file (RECEERR-FILE) for sequential error output
Version history spanning 2007-2015 with many revisions for Japanese health insurance reform compliance
verdict.notes: The file contains extensive Japanese text in comments that has been decoded as latin-1, producing mojibake (garbled characters). The actual encoding is likely EUC-JP or Shift-JIS. The COPY statements reference external copybooks (.INC files) that are not included in this file. The program is clearly part of the well-known JMA ORCA open-source medical receipt software project used in Japanese medical practices. The absence of COMP-3 is somewhat unusual for financial/billing software but may reflect a deliberate style choice or platform constraint.
